I never opened the Gill, Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin, NET Bible, Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* or Augustine (newadvent.org) pages. As you asked, the notes below cover only what those pages actually say.

Many points come from Guzik's Enduring Word commentary, which quotes other writers. Those are marked "(cited by Guzik)" because I didn't read those writers' own works.

---

## Introduction

- This is one of the "Egyptian Hallel" psalms (Psalms 113–118). Jesus sang these psalms with his disciples on the night he was arrested (Matthew 26:30; Mark 14:26). Guzik reads the whole psalm with that night in mind. G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) calls it a song of triumph over death that Christ hands on to his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** The psalm opens with plain, thankful love for God, because God answered prayer in a desperate time. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) rejects the idea that loving God for his gifts is "mercenary." He says no creature can love its Creator any other way. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) says love for God has its eyes open: there are good reasons for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 2:** "I will call on Him as long as I live" is a promise never to pray to any other god. Kidner (cited by Guzik) calls it a decision to trust and worship this God alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 3:**
- The crisis might have been sickness, injury or persecution.
- Kidner (cited by Guzik) explains that Old Testament poetry pictures death and Sheol as attackers that grab the living. The trouble could have been serious illness, or a hurtful betrayal (v. 11 hints at this), or both, as with Job.
- Peter uses "pains of death" for what Christ was freed from at his resurrection (Acts 2:24). Guzik sees a prophetic, messianic meaning here.
- Clarke (cited by Guzik) suggests the "cords" picture prisoners' chains, a condemned man's ropes, or the cloths wrapped around a corpse.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 4:** The prayer goes straight to God, is deeply felt, and names its need plainly. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) calls it short, humble and earnest, a model for prayer, and says real trouble produces real prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 5:** After being rescued, the psalmist praises God as gracious, righteous and merciful. Guzik notes that Jesus sang this before his suffering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 6:**
- Poole (cited by Guzik): "the simple" are sincere, honest people. They don't use tricks to save themselves but wait for God. The world just thinks they are foolish.
- Kidner (cited by Guzik): it is humble of the psalmist to count himself among them, and humble of God to care for them.
- Boice (cited by Guzik): God cares for ordinary people. Jesus called fishermen, and the angels appeared to shepherds.
- Trapp (cited by Guzik): "He saved me" is knowing God by experience, not just from the map of Scripture.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 7:** The soul goes back to the rest it had before the crisis. Edersheim (cited by Guzik via Spurgeon) notes that "rest" is plural in Hebrew, meaning complete rest. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) says a believer who loses peace should look for it again in the Lord alone, not in the world or in their own experience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 8:** The rescue from death, tears and stumbling was as great as the danger. Maclaren (cited by Guzik) says doubt and fear do not prove that trust is absent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 9:** Kidner (cited by Guzik) compares "walk before the LORD" to "walk in the light": you are fully exposed to God, but also fully befriended. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) says the godly person lives aware that God sees everything, rather than living for human opinion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 10:**
- The psalmist trusted God even while deeply distressed.
- Paul quotes this line in 2 Corinthians 4:13. Kidner (cited by Guzik) notes that Paul follows the Greek Septuagint wording, which is stronger than the Hebrew. Both versions still make faith, though hard-pressed, the root of what is said.
- VanGemeren (cited by Guzik) reports Walter Kaiser's view that the same Holy Spirit worked faith in the psalmist, in Paul and in all Christians.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 11:** Guzik treats "All men are liars" as a conclusion reached too quickly, which the psalmist knew was too harsh. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) says it is true in one sense: everyone fails us if we trust them too much, some through dishonesty and others through weakness. He also warns that hasty words are easier said than taken back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 12:** The psalmist asks why God has been so good, not why trouble came. Guzik compares him to the one healed leper who came back to give thanks (Luke 17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 13:**
- Thankfulness starts by *receiving*. Boice (cited by Guzik): the only way to "repay" God is to take even more from him.
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) applies this to the Lord's Supper ("the sacramental table") and to receiving the covenant by faith.
- Morgan (cited by Guzik) sees taking the cup as a pledge of loyalty. He links it to the cup in Gethsemane, which Christ drank in sorrow and then filled with blessing.
- Guzik connects it to the cup of the new covenant (Luke 22:20).

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 14:** This is a public thanksgiving, perhaps with a sacrifice at the temple. Trapp (cited by Guzik) says a lawful vow is a debt to be paid. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) tells how the martyr John Philpot, at his execution, applied "I will pay my vows" to Smithfield, where he was burned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 15:**
- **Ellicott** says this restates Psalm 72:14. He asks why death comes up at this point. His suggestion is that the psalm may be a thanksgiving by survivors of a battle, who remember their dead. https://biblehub.com/psalms/116-15.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary**: the death of a saint matters deeply to God, who sets the day and circumstances of each person's death (citing Psalm 68:20). https://biblehub.com/psalms/116-15.htm
- **Maclaren** (cited by Guzik): God does not lightly allow his saints to die. **Boice** (cited by Guzik): God comes especially close to the dying, and often steps in to spare them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/
- **Spurgeon's sermon "Precious Deaths"**: for the saint, death has lost its sting and is a privilege, not a punishment. This applies to every saint, from a famous preacher to a friendless pauper dying alone. Faith is tested and made perfect in death. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/precious-deaths/
- **Bible Hub Q&A pages** say the Hebrew word *yaqar* means valuable or costly, and "saints" (*chasidim*) means God's faithful, covenant people. They argue the verse doesn't make death less sad. It shows God's care, and believers' deaths lead into his presence and resurrection. https://biblehub.com/q/does_psalm_116_15_lessen_death's_tragedy.htm ; https://biblehub.com/q/what_does_'precious_is_their_death'_mean.htm
- **Martyrdom**: Bible Hub's study note links the verse to martyrdom. https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/116-15.htm ; Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) applies it to martyrs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 16:**
- God's breaking of the bonds leads the psalmist to serve him.
- Clarke (cited by Guzik) reads this as the freed slave of Exodus 21:5–6, who chooses to stay with his master for life.
- Manton (cited by Guzik via Spurgeon): be thankful for godly parents.
- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik): having godly parents doesn't make you godly, since "grace does not run in the blood."

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**v. 17:** We are back at the altar for the thanksgiving sacrifice, calling on God alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

**vv. 18–19:**
- Repeating the vow keeps the scene public, in the temple courts.
- Maclaren (cited by Guzik): a person suffers alone, but joy and thankfulness want company and listeners.
- The closing "Hallelujah" is both personal praise and a call for others to join in.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-116/

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found nothing on this. My sources quote writers from several traditions: Spurgeon (Baptist), Clarke (Methodist), Boice (Presbyterian), and Kidner, Trapp and Poole. They broadly agree, and none of them describes a disagreement between traditions on any verse.

One tradition-specific point did come up. Spurgeon applies v. 13 to "the sacramental table." But I found no Lutheran, Reformed or other teacher setting out a different view of that verse to compare with it.

## 3. Other views

I found nothing. I couldn't read the NET Bible notes, Augustine's exposition at newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I found no pages on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this psalm. The only point close to a "modern scholarship" view is Ellicott's suggestion (above, v. 15) that this was a community song after a battle, and Ellicott is an older commentary.
